content: A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), also referred to as tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 13 (TNFSF13), is a protein that belongs to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily. It is recognized by the cell surface receptor TACI (transmembrane activator and calcium-modulator and cyclophilin ligand interactor). In the cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature, APRIL is classified as CD256. The protein encoded by the TNFSF13 gene is a member of the TNF ligand family. It acts as a ligand for TNFRSF17, also known as BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen), which is a receptor in the TNF receptor family. Both APRIL and its receptor play a critical role in the development of B cells. Experimental studies conducted in vivo have demonstrated that APRIL is essential for the long-term survival of plasma cells within the bone marrow. Mice that are genetically deficient in APRIL exhibit normal immune system development. However, these APRIL-deficient mice show a diminished capacity to support the survival of plasma cells. In vitro studies have indicated that APRIL may induce apoptosis by interacting with other members of the TNF receptor family, such as TNFRSF6 (commonly known as FAS) and TNFRSF14 (also referred to as HVEM). Additionally, three distinct isoforms of APRIL, resulting from alternative splicing of its transcript, have been identified. APRIL has been shown to interact with TNFRSF13B (also known as TACI) and B-cell activating factor (BAFF). From a clinical perspective, APRIL is being investigated as a therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases and B-cell-related malignancies. Notably, at least one monoclonal antibody targeting APRIL has progressed to phase I clinical trials for the treatment of multiple myeloma.
